<reason>CON built a tighter path to victory by exploiting the exact wording of the motion: PRO must show benefit outweighs long-term regret/harm, and CON kept forcing PRO to admit the evidentiary gaps that make that comparison unprovable. The decisive exchange was CON's R2 "fork" — PRO's positive follow-up data comes from adolescents who completed hormone treatment, not from the "carefully screened, reversible pause" population the motion contemplates, and PRO had already conceded no validated criterion separates true persisters from adolescents whose identity might shift. PRO's response (screening's function is "improving present decisions," not certifying the future; delay has its own harms) was reasonable and kept the debate live, but it never squarely closed the mismatch between the studied population and the "carefully screened" population the motion asks about, and PRO's closing pivoted to generalities ("clairvoyance") rather than directly re-engaging that specific charge. CON's closing crystallized this into a clean burden-of-proof frame that PRO didn't fully rebut. CON loses some credit for having two turns clipped for length, which cost it clean closure on a couple of points, but the surviving content still carried the more decisive rebuttal arc.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's R2 fork in [A4.1]-[A4.2]: PRO's benefit evidence comes from patients who proceeded through hormones, so PRO cannot simultaneously claim the safety of a reversible pause and the evidentiary support attached to the full pathway. PRO's answer (screening doesn't need to predict lifelong identity to be a safeguard) mitigated but did not fully resolve this mismatch by closing.</best_rebuttal>
